rationale: Data from the 8 ADHD-200 sites differs a lot because of scanners and protocols. Those site shifts take up most of the variance in the connectivity features, while scoring compares subjects only within each site. I'll standardize each site's features separately (mean and SD from that site's training subjects only), which removes the site offsets so the L2 logistic regression can focus on differences within each site.

I'm replacing the Fisher-z Pearson correlations with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariance matrices, computed on the standardized CC200 time series. Short, site-dependent scan lengths with 200 ROIs give noisy correlation estimates. In benchmarks (Dadi et al., 2019), shrinkage plus a Riemannian tangent projection around a label-free group mean beat raw correlations for rs-fMRI phenotype prediction. All-zero ROIs are handled because they get unit variance after standardizing, and shrinkage keeps every matrix positive definite.

I'm replacing the single global reference with per-site Riemannian re-centering, which does not use labels. Each subject's Ledoit-Wolf covariance is whitened by its own site's Riemannian mean (C → M_site^{-1/2} C M_site^{-1/2}) before the tangent-space projection. Scanner and protocol differences act on the covariance matrices themselves, so this harmonizes them geometrically on the SPD manifold (Riemannian Procrustes / parallel transport, Zanini et al. 2018; Yger et al.). That differs from round 1's per-site z-scoring of Pearson features, which failed. All sites then share the identity as reference, so the classifier can learn within-site connectivity deviations.

I'm combining several atlases. The same Ledoit-Wolf tangent-space pipeline runs on CC200, AAL and Harvard-Oxford, with one L2 logistic regression per atlas, and their predicted probabilities are averaged. Each parcellation captures ADHD-related connectivity differently and with different noise. Benchmarks such as Dadi et al. 2019 and the ABIDE/ADHD multi-atlas work found that averaging across atlases reduces variance in this p >> n setting. Each item's first columns record the block sizes, so `fit_predict` can split the concatenated features reliably.

I'm adding a second, small model on relative per-ROI amplitude, a proxy for ALFF. It uses the log SD of each ROI's band-passed signal minus the subject's median log SD, which cancels each scanner's global scaling. Its standardized log-odds are blended 0.3/0.7 with the existing tangent-space model. ALFF changes are a well-replicated finding in ADHD (Zang 2007), and the current pipeline throws this information away, because it z-scores each ROI's time series before estimating covariance.

I'm adding global brain connectivity (GBC) to the per-ROI "nodal" model, next to relative ALFF. GBC is each ROI's mean Fisher-z correlation with all other valid ROIs, minus the subject's median GBC. ADHD studies report changed hub strength (DMN, frontoparietal, cerebellar), and this 200-feature summary is a low-variance view of it that the 19,900-dimensional tangent model can't estimate stably at n≈700. Subtracting the subject's median cancels global shifts in correlation (for example from motion or scanner differences), the same way the ALFF features are normalized.

I'm adding a third small regional model based on each ROI's lag-1 autocorrelation (Fisher-z, minus the subject's median), blended with the existing models as connectivity 0.6, amplitude 0.25, autocorrelation 0.15. This feature is a proxy for fALFF and Hurst-type spectral slope: it measures how much of each region's band-passed power sits in its slowest fluctuations. ADHD reports describe changed slow-band fluctuations (Zang 2007; Sato 2012), and neither the z-scored covariances nor the log-SD feature captures this. Subtracting the subject's median removes the dependence on TR and site, and scoring within site means TR is constant within each comparison.

I'm adding relative ALFF from the finer CC400 parcellation (~392 ROIs) alongside the CC200 ALFF in the amplitude model. Both use subject-median-normalized log SD and feed a single L2 logistic model. Relative ALFF is our best low-dimensional signal (+0.015), and ADHD amplitude effects are reported in small structures such as the striatum, cerebellar vermis, precuneus and ACC. A two-scale view should localize those effects better than CC200 alone, while keeping the feature count far below the tangent model's.

I'm adding relative ALFF (subject-median-normalized log ROI SD) from the anatomical AAL and Harvard-Oxford atlases to the amplitude model, next to CC200 and CC400. These atlases mark out the caudate, putamen, thalamus and cerebellar vermis as whole regions, and those are central to ADHD amplitude findings. The data-driven CC atlases split or blur them. Amplitude features are low-dimensional, so adding atlases is much cheaper and less noisy than the multi-atlas connectivity tried in round 4.

ADHD prevalence varies a lot between ADHD-200 sites, and the metric only compares subjects within a site. So the classifiers can currently lower their loss by learning site/scanner signatures as "ADHD" directions, which spends their limited capacity on signal the metric ignores. I'll fit both logistic models with sample weights that balance the two classes within each site (single-class sites get a small weight). This makes site carry no label information during training. Features are unchanged, unlike the per-site standardization and re-centering that failed in rounds 1 and 3.

The regularization strengths (C=0.001 for connectivity, C=0.01 for amplitude) and the 0.3 amplitude blend weight were all set by hand. This change picks them in each training fold with a grouped inner 5-fold CV over subjects, scored by within-site AUROC, which is the harness metric. A small grid of three C values per model and four blend weights keeps the search cheap. On ties, the current defaults win, which limits overfitting from a noisy inner CV.

This adds a multi-scale connectivity branch: a log-Euclidean tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf covariances on the finer CC400 parcellation (about 77k edges), mixed with the CC200 tangent logits. Inner grouped CV chooses the mixing weight from {0, 0.33, 0.5}, so the branch can drop out if it doesn't help. Multi-scale amplitude was kept (round 8) because finer parcels localize ADHD effects in small structures such as the striatum, cerebellum and ACC. Round 4's multi-atlas attempt failed with untuned equal averaging of anatomical atlases, which is different from a tuned, nested CC200/CC400 combination.

ADHD children move more and differ in global arousal and signal quality, and this is one of the most robust ADHD/TD differences in the measured rs-fMRI. The current pipeline removes it, because it standardizes the time series and subtracts each subject's median amplitude. I'll add six global signal-quality scalars to the amplitude block, each z-scored per site with that site's training statistics (no labels used). They are global amplitude, DVARS level, DVARS spike fraction, DVARS tail ratio, relative derivative power and global coherence. Because they are z-scored within site, only within-site differences remain, which is what the metric scores.

This adds a third, low-dimensional branch built from network-level connectivity. The CC200 ROIs are grouped into 20 networks by ward clustering of the group-mean Fisher-z connectome, which uses no labels. Each subject's Fisher-z correlations are then averaged within and between networks (210 features) and fed to their own L2 logistic model, whose C and blend weight (including 0) are tuned in the existing grouped inner CV. ADHD effects are mostly reported at the network level (weaker DMN/task-positive anticorrelation, frontostriatal and cerebellar coupling). Averaging hundreds of noisy edges per block should estimate these more stably than the 19,900-edge tangent model can at n≈700. This is a different granularity from the nodal GBC summary that failed in round 6.

I'm adding a second CC200 tangent-space connectivity model, built from time series with the global signal regressed out, and averaging its logits 50/50 with the existing model. Both use the same C, so the inner-CV grid gets no larger. The ADHD-200 data only offers the no-GSR strategy, and its correlations are dominated by a shared global component (arousal, motion, scanner), which hides specific edges. An ensemble of the GSR and no-GSR views should cut the variance from that nuisance without throwing away whatever signal the global component carries.

Before estimating the CC200 Ledoit-Wolf covariance, I'll drop motion- or artifact-corrupted frames: those whose DVARS (frame-to-frame RMS signal change) is a robust outlier within the subject, with at most 20% of frames removed. This "scrubbing" follows Power et al. 2012. ADHD children move more, and the spike frames add spurious distance-dependent correlation that swamps the neural connectivity signal. Round 13 showed motion proxies don't help as predictors, so cleaning them out of the connectivity estimate should sharpen the tangent-space model. The ALFF features stay unchanged.

I'm adding a proxy for regional homogeneity (ReHo) to the nodal amplitude model. The CC400 parcels sit nested inside CC200 parcels, so each CC400 ROI gets a "parent": the CC200 ROI it correlates with most on average across all subjects, which uses no labels. The feature is the Fisher-z correlation of each CC400 ROI with its parent, minus the subject's median. This measures how coherent the signal is at a local scale, which neither the z-scored tangent connectivity nor log-amplitude captures. Altered local coherence is a replicated ADHD finding (Cao 2006; Zang 2007), and subtracting the subject's median cancels global smoothness and scanner effects.

I'm adding local functional connectivity density (lFCD) to the nodal model, extending the ReHo proxy that was kept in round 17. For each CC400 ROI, the new feature is its mean Fisher-z correlation with its k=6 nearest functional neighbours, minus the subject's median. The neighbours are chosen without labels, as the ROIs with the highest correlation in the all-subject mean connectome. Tomasi & Volkow (2012) found altered lFCD in ADHD. This captures coherence in a neighbourhood around each parcel, which sits between the parent-only ReHo that helped (round 17) and the whole-brain GBC that failed (round 6).

I'm adding a second, coarser level of the regional-homogeneity proxy that was kept in round 17. Each CC200 parcel gets a "parent": the AAL anatomical region it correlates with most across all subjects, chosen without labels. The new feature is the Fisher-z correlation of each parcel with that parent, minus the subject's median, and it goes into the nodal model. Altered local coherence in ADHD (Cao 2006; Zang 2007) is reported across spatial scales. A two-level ReHo hierarchy (CC400→CC200 and CC200→AAL) mirrors the multi-scale ALFF that was kept in round 8, and it uses only 200 extra low-noise features.

Inner-CV within-site AUROC on about 560 subjects has a standard error of roughly 0.02, much larger than the gaps between neighbouring grid points. So picking the single best (C_conn, C_amp, w) mostly chases fold noise and adds variance across outer folds. Instead of the argmax, I'll average the blended standardized logits of the 5 best inner-CV configurations, which keeps the gain from tuning while lowering the variance of the selection.
